cases.title: Gas Flaring at Rumaila and Zubair Oil Fields, Basra
cases.place: Rumaila and Zubair oil fields, Basra, Iraq
cases.point: Rumaila oil field, south-west of Basra (approximate centre of the field)

lenders.name: BP (United Kingdom) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Holds a 47.6% stake in the Rumaila Operating Organization, which runs the field under BP's supervision as lead contractor (S&P Global, 2021). BP says the operating organisation is the operator and that BP is a shareholder giving technical advice.

lenders.name: Eni (Italy) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Leads the Zubair consortium with about 32.81% under a 20-year technical service contract (RTTNews, 2010); the BBC calls it the lead contractor.

cases.conditions: No lender condition. Iraq's government owns the fields; foreign oil companies hold stakes and work them under contract. Iraqi law bans flaring within six miles of homes, and the BBC found flares less than two miles from front doors.

companies.name: BP
companies.role: 47.6% stake in the Rumaila Operating Organization and lead contractor (S&P Global)

companies.name: Eni
companies.role: About 32.81% stake and lead of the Zubair consortium (RTTNews)

cases.community: A leaked Iraqi Health Ministry report seen by BBC Arabic blames air pollution for a 20% rise in cancer in Basra from 2015 to 2018. BBC tests of urine from 52 children found 70% had raised levels of 2-naphthol, a form of naphthalene. Air tests over two weeks in five communities found benzene at or above Iraq's limit in at least four. Fatima Falah Najem lived 1.6 miles from the nearest flares and died of leukaemia at 13. Ali Hussein Julood, who grew up near Rumaila, was diagnosed with leukaemia at 15 in 2017 and died on 21 April 2023, aged 21 (Hausfeld). Locals call the town of North Rumaila "the cemetery" (BBC).
cases.suppression: The BBC reported a confidential order from Iraq's prime minister banning government employees from speaking about health damage from pollution. Filming permits for Rumaila were denied, and a team member was threatened by intelligence officers and left the project (GIJN).
cases.killed_note: None counted. The deaths of Ali Hussein Julood and Fatima Falah Najem are tied to flaring by the BBC's reporting and, for Ali, by his father's legal claim; no court ruling on the cause was found.
cases.outcome: On 22 April 2024 Ali's father, Hussein Julood, sent BP a letter before action (Hausfeld). BP said it would review the concerns raised by the BBC.

sources.title: BP in oil field where 'cancer is rife'
sources.publisher: The Star (Kenya), carrying a BBC report

sources.title: How a BBC Investigation Exposed the Impact of Gas Flaring on Iraqi Communities
In a historic first, BP hit by legal action alleging that its excessive gas flaring caused death of young Iraqi
Iraq approves spinoff of BP-operated Rumaila oil field
Iraq
Eni-led Consortium To Develop Iraq's Zubair Oil Field - Update

cases.confidence_note: The link is documented; what is disputed is responsibility and cause of illness. BP told the BBC it reports flaring only where it is operator and that Rumaila's data are not in its reporting. It said it was "extremely concerned" and would review. Eni rejects any claim that it endangers health. The health figures come from BBC tests and a leaked report, not a published epidemiological study.
cases.ecosystem: Satellite data show Rumaila burning more gas than any other site in the world (BBC). Benzene was measured in the air near the fields.

lvwhy.project: Oil extraction with routine gas flaring close to homes.

cases.title: Ras El-Hekma Evictions for the Abu Dhabi Deal
cases.point: Ras El-Hekma on Egypt's north coast (approximate); evictions were reported in villages such as Al-Hashayma

lenders.name: Abu Dhabi Developmental Holding Company (ADQ) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Signed the Ras El-Hekma deal with Egypt's government in February 2024, valued at an estimated $35 billion (Al-Manassa).

cases.conditions: No loan condition. The land was cleared for a development deal between Egypt's government and an Abu Dhabi state holding company.

companies.name: Abu Dhabi Developmental Holding Company (ADQ)
companies.role: Investor in the Ras El-Hekma development

cases.community: Residents, including Bedouin families, told Al-Manassa they were paid on 2018 valuations. Moussa Khamis of Al-Hashayma faces no more than 150,000 pounds per feddan; one resident set this against a market price of 2 million pounds a feddan. A 2024 deal reportedly raised the rate to 300,000 pounds per feddan. Tribal elder Ibrahim Sangar alleges some officials block claims unless paid bribes; this is not independently verified. Displaced families were offered 1,000 square metres each in Shams El-Hekma, which residents call too small to sustain their livelihoods. Resident Qaddoura Al-Ajni says families have been scattered to Shams El-Hekma, southern Matrouh and southern El-Dabaa.
cases.suppression: Moussa Khamis says he woke on the second day of Ramadan to bulldozers and security forces around his home in Al-Hashayma and was told to leave at once (Al-Manassa). No arrests are reported in the pages cited.
cases.outcome: On 28 February 2025 Scene Now reported over EGP 6 billion paid to residents for relocation, with demolitions discussed at a government meeting, and housing and land titling under way at Shams El-Hekma.

sources.title: The hidden toll of Ras El-Hekma
Over EGP 6 Billion Disbursed to Ras El-Hekma Residents for Relocation

cases.confidence_note: Government and residents differ on whether compensation is fair. Neither source gives the number of people moved. Individual eviction accounts come from one outlet; the government's own meeting report confirms relocation payments and demolitions.

lvwhy.land: Bedouin land taken for a foreign-funded coastal development.

cases.title: Damietta Fertiliser Plant Protests
cases.point: Damietta port area, near the plant (approximate)

lenders.name: Agrium (Canada) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Signed a 2006 deal for a fertiliser plant at Ras El-Bar, with $1.2 billion expected. After protests the original plan was cancelled in 2008 and Agrium took a 26% stake in state-owned MOPCO (Ahram Online).

cases.conditions: No loan condition. Agrium threatened international arbitration when a parliamentary committee recommended moving the plant to Suez (Ahram Online).

companies.name: Agrium (now Nutrien)
companies.role: 26% shareholder in MOPCO from 2008

cases.community: Residents of Damietta, whose economy depends largely on fishing and fish farming, said the plant harmed animals, plants, fish and health (Ahram Online). No pollution measurements appear in the reports cited; a protest statement says a local committee found the plant caused many diseases (Platform).
cases.suppression: On 13 November 2011 clashes began at dawn. Protesters had blocked the port and almost all roads in the city (MENA, via Ahram Online). Platform reports 25 arrests, with those held released after protesters besieged an army unit, and at least one protester killed and many injured.
cases.killed_note: Uncounted. Islam Abdallah was killed on 13 November 2011. An eyewitness told Ahram Online police and army killed him; Platform says police or military. No official finding was found, and no source opened says the forces were guarding or clearing for the plant: protesters had blocked the port and roads. Ahram Online's headline says two died; other reports say one.
cases.outcome: Platform reports the government was forced to shut the plant, but the dispute continued. A later settlement ended a 12-year dispute: Nutrien (formerly Agrium) transferred its MOPCO shares to Egypt's finance ministry, with total gross proceeds of $540 million (Ahram Online).

sources.title: Update: Egypt army and police kill two in clashes in Damietta over factory saga
Five years on, Damietta's Agrium controversy reignites
Mass environmental justice uprising engulfs Damietta on Egypt's Mediterranean coast
The deal put an end to a 12-year dispute between Egypt and the Nutrien Ltd company (formerly Agrium Inc)

cases.confidence_note: The company denied harm, citing a Ministry of Environment report and offering a WHO inspection. Agrium held 26% of state-owned MOPCO in 2011 and was not the operator, though Ahram Online calls the plant Canadian-Egyptian. The death and arrests are reported by a witness and one campaign group; pollution damage is claimed by residents and was not measured. Ahram Online notes some observers tied the opposition to landowners and businessmen with interests in Ras El-Bar.

lvwhy.project: Foreign-backed fertiliser plant built beside a fishing community.

cases.title: Tangier Candle Protests against Amendis (Veolia)
cases.point: Place des Nations, Tangier, where several thousand protesters gathered (African Energy); coordinates approximate

lenders.name: Veolia Environnement (France) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Its affiliate Amendis has run water, wastewater and electricity in Tangier and Tetouan since 2002 (Reuters).

cases.conditions: No loan condition. Amendis says its bills reflect a 2014 pricing structure from the government's rescue programme for the state power utility, and peak summer demand (Reuters).

companies.name: Veolia Environnement
companies.role: Owner of Amendis, concession holder in Tangier and Tetouan

cases.community: About 1.5 million bills issued since summer 2015 needed revision and default notices were suspended (African Energy). In an undated account from Tangier, one resident's bill for a 60-square-metre flat jumped almost 500%, costing in one year the equivalent of 4 years at the old rates (Gerald Loftus). Protesters marched with candles on successive weekends.
cases.suppression: Authorities used water cannons on protesters (The Moroccan Times). A government statement warned citizens against those it said wanted to make mischief (Reuters).
cases.outcome: Tangier's mayor promised bills since July would be revised (African Energy). The interior minister ordered a fast review. Before the protests, Veolia dropped a planned sale of its Moroccan businesses to Actis for about 370 million euros after local authorities blocked it, and agreed to review its concession contracts (Reuters).

sources.title: Defiant Moroccans protest over water, power prices (Reuters)
Price rise protests in northern Morocco
Tangier: second weekend of huge protests against Amendis (title from the page address)
Your Choice: Electricity, Food, or Shelter

cases.confidence_note: Crowd sizes differ: The Moroccan Times cites local reports of at least 60,000; Reuters says thousands. Amendis blames a 2014 state pricing change and summer demand. The only per-household figure is one resident's account on an undated page, so it may not be from 2015.

lvwhy.priv: City utilities run by a foreign concession holder.
lvwhy.prices: Bills rose sharply and 1.5 million had to be revised.

cases.title: Lafarge Payments to Armed Groups, Jalabiyeh Cement Plant

lenders.name: Lafarge SA (France) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Built the plant for about $680 million and ran it from about May 2010 to September 2014 through Lafarge Cement Syria (NPR).

cases.conditions: No loan condition. Lafarge pleaded guilty in the United States in October 2022 to conspiring to give material support to ISIS and the al-Nusrah Front, covering August 2013 to October 2014.

companies.name: Lafarge SA
companies.role: Owner of Lafarge Cement Syria; bought by Holcim in 2015

cases.community: At least a dozen workers were kidnapped from 2012 to the end of 2014 (New York Times). Lafarge spent around 200,000 euros to free nine employees seized in autumn 2012. Foreign staff left in summer 2012 while Syrian staff kept working; former staff say managers threatened dismissal even when roads were dangerous. ISIS took the plant in September 2014, and remaining Syrian staff had to flee on their own after buses never returned. Mechanic Abdul al-Homada was kidnapped in Aleppo in 2013 after collecting his pay and was fired for "unjustified absence" (AFP).
cases.killed_note: Uncounted, because the killers were armed groups, not the company. AFP reports mechanic Yassin Ismail was detained by jihadists and executed, according to relatives and former colleagues, and that Abdul al-Homada was very likely killed. The New York Times says the workers it followed all survived, without addressing these two. Lafarge's owner says it has no knowledge of a Lafarge Syria worker dying after abduction and that Homada was taken by the Syrian regime, which a colleague disputes.
cases.outcome: Lafarge agreed to pay about $778 million in the US. Payment figures differ: about $6 million to the groups (NPR), $10.24 million including intermediaries (Business & Human Rights Resource Centre), more than $5 million (New York Times, from French court documents), about 13 million euros (AFP). France's top court upheld a charge of complicity in crimes against humanity but dropped endangering employees, finding Syrian law governs the Syrian workers' contracts (JURIST).

sources.title: French cement giant Larfage pleads guilty in U.S. court to paying millions to ISIS
USA: Lafarge pleads guilty to financially supporting ISIS in Syria & agrees to pay $777.8 million fine
Syria workers say French firm abandoned them (title from the page address)
'ISIS Is Coming!' How a French Company Pushed the Limits in War-Torn Syria (New York Times)
France top court upholds charges of crimes against humanity against manufacturing company

cases.confidence_note: The payments are admitted in a US guilty plea. Whether workers died is disputed between AFP and the company; the New York Times does not report the two men named by AFP. French proceedings are not finished. LafargeHolcim acknowledged "unacceptable errors" in Syria; Holcim says it never operated in Syria and was not involved.

lvwhy.project: A foreign-owned plant kept running in a war zone through payments to armed groups.

cases.title: ArcelorMittal Temirtau Mine Deaths and Air Pollution
cases.point: Temirtau steel plant area (approximate); the mines are near Karaganda

lenders.name: ArcelorMittal, formerly Mittal Steel (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Entered Kazakhstan during the 1990s privatisation, was urged to take the Karmet steel combine, and operated the Temirtau plant from 1996 to December 2023 (SteelWatch; CABAR). The Kostenko mine and seven others belonged to the company (CABAR).

cases.conditions: No loan condition. President Nazarbayev said Karmet had debts of nearly $700 million in the 1990s when he urged the investor to take it (CABAR).

companies.name: ArcelorMittal
companies.role: Owner of ArcelorMittal Temirtau until December 2023

cases.community: A blast at the Kostenko mine on 28 October 2023 killed 46 of 252 people underground; local officials said it happened during a safety system check that fell short of standards (Eurasianet; CABAR). Five died at the Kazakhstanskaya mine in August 2023, and 33 miners died in 2004 (CABAR). The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air estimates air pollution from the plant led to 3,000 deaths, 190 preterm births and 2,600 cases of childhood asthma during ArcelorMittal's operation, costing $4.2 billion in health damage (SteelWatch).
cases.killed_note: 84 counted: the three mine accidents itemised by CABAR, all under this owner: 46 at Kostenko (October 2023), 5 at Kazakhstanskaya (August 2023) and 33 in the coal department mines (2004). No source gives a mine-only total of 100. Broader totals, not counted: more than 100 at all company facilities over 15 years (official figures via Eurasianet), over 140 workers (SteelWatch, citing government and civil society), 180 at its plants over almost 30 years (CABAR). The modelled pollution deaths are not counted.
cases.outcome: After the blast President Tokayev announced an end to investment cooperation with the company. ArcelorMittal left in December 2023, receiving $985 million from a state-owned fund (SteelWatch). The company had typically faced little more than fines (Eurasianet).

sources.title: Why Was ArcelorMittal Temirtau with 180 Fatalities Over 30 Years Asked to Leave Kazakhstan Only Now?
Kazakhstan: Deadly mine disaster hastens ArcelorMittal Temirtau nationalization
ArcelorMittal given golden handshake, left Kazakhstan with multi-billion dollar health costs

cases.confidence_note: Total worker deaths differ by source and period. The pollution figures are a modelled estimate by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, released by SteelWatch. ArcelorMittal says its exit agreement bars it from commenting; in mid-2023 management said nearly 30% of investment went to safety. Analyst Daniyar Ashimbayev also blames worn Soviet-era infrastructure, poor repairs, corruption and absent state oversight.
cases.ecosystem: Air pollution from PM2.5, nitrogen dioxide and sulphur dioxide around Kazakhstan's largest integrated steel plant (SteelWatch).

lvwhy.priv: State steel and coal assets sold to a foreign owner in the 1990s.
lvwhy.project: Mines and a coal-based steel plant run by that owner.

cases.title: Karazhanbas and Ersai Oil Strikes and Jailings

lenders.name: CITIC (China) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: CITIC Oil & Gas Holdings owned 50% of KarazhanbasMunai; KMG EP held the other 50%. It is a subsidiary of CITIC Resources, majority-owned by China's state investment company CITIC Group (Human Rights Watch).

lenders.name: Saipem, part-owned by Eni (Italy) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Saipem International owned 50% of Ersai Caspian Contractor; ERC Holdings held the other 50%. Saipem is partly owned by Eni (Human Rights Watch).

companies.name: CITIC Oil & Gas Holdings
companies.role: 50% owner of KarazhanbasMunai

companies.name: Saipem
companies.role: 50% owner of Ersai Caspian Contractor

cases.community: Oil workers at KarazhanbasMunai struck from 17 May 2011 and about 1,000 were fired. Three companies together fired over 2,000, including the state-owned OzenMunaiGas (Human Rights Watch).
cases.suppression: Natalia Sokolova, the Karazhanbas union lawyer, was barred from arbitration on 21 January 2011 by company representatives, then sentenced in August 2011 to six years in prison for inciting social discord; she was later released. In June 2011 authorities broke the Ersai strike, a court temporarily jailed the five strike committee members and the Karakiya union was suspended for six months.
cases.killed_note: Uncounted here. On 16 December 2011 police fired on a crowd in Zhanaozen, killing at least 12 by government figures; prosecutors said three others died in the clashes. That strike was at OzenMunaiGas, which is wholly state-owned, not at the foreign-owned firms.
cases.outcome: After the Zhanaozen shootings, 34 people were convicted in June 2012 and 13 received prison terms.

sources.title: Striking Oil, Striking Workers: Violations of Labor Rights in Kazakhstan's Oil Sector

cases.confidence_note: Rests on one Human Rights Watch report. Ersai told Human Rights Watch it has a long history of constructive bargaining but did not address the harassment claims; KarazhanbasMunai and Saipem did not reply. The foreign owners held half of each firm, and the arrests and sentences were the state's. The case stays because of the jailings, not the dismissals alone.

lvwhy.labour: Strikers at part foreign-owned oil firms were fired and union figures jailed.

cases.title: ArcelorMittal Zenica Steelworks Pollution

lenders.name: ArcelorMittal, then Mittal Steel (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Bought 92% of the ironworks in 2004 from the Kuwait Investment Agency and the Federal Government; the privatisation agreement was never disclosed (Heinrich Böll Foundation).

cases.conditions: No loan condition on the sale. The company's reported obligation was $165 million of investment over 10 years. Plans submitted in 2008, due by end 2011, were still partly unfinished more than five years later (The Guardian via The Ferret). A new heating plant begun in 2019 is partly financed by an EBRD loan (Böll); no source ties that loan to the pollution.

companies.name: ArcelorMittal
companies.role: Owner of ArcelorMittal Zenica

cases.community: The Federal Institute for Agropedology earlier discouraged growing crops or raising livestock near the plant, and an official said lettuce, spinach and vegetables take up heavy metals. Soil samples taken by the reporting group CIN from more than 50 sites, including gardens, schools and clinics, in March 2024 were heavily contaminated with pollutants including arsenic and lead (OCCRP). Local resident Šahiza Šehić says almost every house has lost someone to cancer; no detailed study links Zenica's air to cancer (The Guardian).
cases.killed_note: None counted; no study attributes deaths to the plant.
cases.outcome: A 2023 federal inspection found deadlines missed for at least 13 of 15 required anti-pollution measures. From 2019 to 2024 fines totalled $79,751; 87 inspections led to at least 46 violations (OCCRP). Eco Forum Zenica filed criminal charges in 2015; the investigation was suspended in November 2020 for insufficient evidence. The coke plant's closure was announced in March 2024.

sources.title: Leaked Report Highlights Pollution Problems at ArcelorMittal's Bosnian Steelworks
The Bosnian steel town choking to death (The Guardian)
Rusting promises and a judicial marathon

cases.confidence_note: ArcelorMittal blames earlier operators, especially in the 1980s, for soil contamination, and the town's heating and home coal burning for sulphur dioxide. It says it has invested 107 million euros in environmental protection since 2004, admits some measures came late, and says the coke plant closure cut diffuse emissions by 80%.
cases.ecosystem: Days with sulphur dioxide over the daily limit fell from 252 in 2014 to 117 in 2019; the legal maximum is 3 (Böll). Heavy metals were found in soil, slag was dumped without permits, and sludge may have reached the Bosna River (OCCRP).

lvwhy.priv: Steelworks sold to a foreign owner on undisclosed terms.
lvwhy.project: Plant ran for years past its emission deadlines.

cases.title: Söyüdlü Protest at the Gadabay Gold Mine
cases.point: Söyüdlü village near the Gadabay mine (approximate)

lenders.name: Anglo Asian Mining (United Kingdom) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: UK-registered company that runs the Gadabay (Gedabek) gold mine through its subsidiary AIMC (Eurasianet; Meydan TV). Its top shareholder is Iranian-American businessman Reza Vaziri with 27.8% (Eurasianet). Under the contract the government takes a 51% share of revenue (Meydan TV).

companies.name: Anglo Asian Mining
companies.role: Operator of the Gadabay mine

cases.community: Residents said a lake in the village had been used for about 11 years to hold mine waste, and blamed it for breathing problems, lung damage and cancer (OC Media; Eurasianet). They protested plans for a second waste lake. These are residents' accounts; no measurements appear in the pages cited.
cases.suppression: On 20 June 2023 riot police used tear gas and rubber bullets (Eurasianet), and a video showed a 78-year-old woman pepper-sprayed as she walked away; a ministry spokesman said the officer committed a serious offence (OC Media). About 15 were reportedly injured and ten detained (OC Media); later reports say 10 injured or 11 arrested. Witnesses say at least seven were held for 20 days and one was fined 1,500 manats (about $880). Roads to the village were closed to non-residents. Two journalists were reportedly detained. Former lawmaker Nazim Baydamirli, who backed the protesters, was arrested within weeks and was later given eight years for extortion (Eurasianet).
cases.outcome: The prime minister suspended the mine on 13 July 2023 pending an audit by an international company; Anglo Asian denied the government's allegations and agreed to re-evaluate its second dam. On 5 August 2024 the company was authorised to restart after just over a year, and the government approved the waste dam expansion (Eurasianet; Meydan TV).

sources.title: Crackdown on environmental protest in Azerbaijan sparks outrage
Azerbaijani police lock down village after environmental protests
Azerbaijan temporarily closes gold mine run by UK-registered company
Protests in Soyudlu raise concern over mining operations, influence, and corruption
Azerbaijan: Ex-MP gets an eight-year sentence for voicing support for former constituents
Azerbaijani government approves cyanide lake expansion in Soyudlu village despite last year's protests
Aliyevs' Secret Mining Empire

cases.confidence_note: The outside owner is real. OC Media says OCCRP found the mines were owned by President Aliyev's two daughters, but OCCRP's 2016 report ties them to a separate consortium around the Chovdar mine and describes Gedebey as a site of the company now called Anglo Asian. Pollution harm is claimed by residents and not measured; the district head called it disinformation. The Interior Ministry says several workers were injured. Anglo Asian denied the government's allegations.
cases.ecosystem: Residents say cyanide from the waste lake contaminated their drinking water and protest signs said the Kura river was being poisoned. Unmeasured.

lvwhy.project: Waste lake for a foreign-operated gold mine.

cases.title: Linglong Tyre Factory Workers, Zrenjanin
cases.point: Zrenjanin, site of the Linglong plant (town centre; plant location approximate)

lenders.name: Linglong Tire (China) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Chinese-owned $940 million plant on 100 hectares of state land given free. Linglong received just over $247 million in state allocations from 2020 to 2024, including at least $89 million in direct subsidies, by RFE/RL's account of its financial report.

companies.name: Linglong Tire
companies.role: Owner of the Zrenjanin plant

cases.community: About 500 Vietnamese workers were on site in 2021, according to the European Parliament; the A11 Initiative says over 400. A11 and ASTRA visited and concluded labour rights were seriously violated and health and possibly lives were at risk, with trafficking for labour exploitation a strong possibility. RFE/RL reported overcrowded dormitories, food served on the floor, wages months late and seized passports. Eleven Indian men later alleged trafficking and labour exploitation, and received back pay, compensation and tickets (Astra, via RFE/RL).
cases.outcome: The European Parliament adopted a resolution on 16 December 2021 by 586 to 53, with 44 abstentions. On 18 December 2025 US customs announced a withhold release order blocking imports from the plant, citing confiscated passports, withheld wages and abusive conditions (RFE/RL). Serbia's anti-trafficking centre verbally declared the Vietnamese case closed, saying it could not communicate with the workers before they left.

sources.title: Serbia's Prized Chinese Tire Factory Faces US Blockade Amid Forced Labor Concerns (RFE/RL)
Resolution on forced labour in the Linglong factory and environmental protests in Serbia
The European Parliament's Resolution Appealing to Serbian Authorities to Investigate the Case of Vietnamese Workers

cases.confidence_note: Linglong denies responsibility for 2021-22, saying the workers were employed by subcontractors, rejects the Indian men's claims, and has not publicly addressed the US order. The European Parliament calls these serious allegations. President Vučić calls the criticism a media-political campaign. The US order is an import ban on stated evidence, not a court verdict.

lvwhy.labour: Migrant workers at a foreign-owned plant reportedly had passports seized and pay withheld.

cases.title: Roșia Montană Buyouts and Gabriel Resources

lenders.name: Gabriel Resources (Canada) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Mining partner in Rosia Montana Gold Corporation, a company formed with the Romanian state (The Black Sea).

lenders.name: ICSID (World Bank Group)
lenders.role: Heard Gabriel's 2015 claim against Romania for at least $3.3 billion and as much as $4.4 billion, about 2% of Romania's GDP (Inequality.org). Romania won in March 2024 (Agerpres).

cases.conditions: No loan condition. Authorities left the expropriation of over 200 households to the company (The Black Sea).

companies.name: Gabriel Resources
companies.role: Canadian partner in the Roșia Montană project company, RMGC; no percentage in the sources cited

cases.community: The company bought homes to clear the site. 125 families moved to Recea, a neighbourhood built near Alba Iulia, and others left for other cities. The local population shrank between 2009 and 2012. Some families split because not all owners would sell. Some residents say they were offered mobile phones, baskets of goods and medical support before selling; one former villager fell into debt. Plans affected graves, three churches and six cemeteries. A regional appeal court ruled that two local councillors had a conflict of interest with the company (The Black Sea).
cases.outcome: A December 2013 report describes MPs rejecting exploration in the Apuseni Mountains, and the government backed down after protests (The Black Sea; Inequality.org). The tribunal ruled for Romania and ordered Gabriel to repay Romania's legal costs (Agerpres).

sources.title: Billion-euro Rosia Montana mine project rips communities apart
People Power in Romania Stopped a Mining Project. Now the Corporation is Suing for Billions of Dollars.
Guvern: România primeşte câştig de cauză la acuzaţiile Gabriel Resources; reclamanţii - obligaţi să plătească despăgubiri

cases.confidence_note: The company says only one of the 125 Recea houses is unoccupied. It was the town's biggest provider of jobs, with unemployment above 70%. Its representative refused to discuss claims it bought goodwill. The sources describe sales rather than forced removals, though authorities left the expropriation of over 200 households to the company.
cases.ecosystem: The plan involved blowing up four mountains and a cyanide tailings pond for at least 250 million tonnes of waste; it was not carried out.

lvwhy.land: A foreign company bought out and emptied much of a village.
lvwhy.project: Open-pit gold mine that was planned but not built.

cases.displaced_note: The Black Sea: 125 families moved to Recea; more sold and left for other cities. Total not given.

cases.title: Bulgaria 2013 Electricity Bill Protests
cases.point: Varna, where protesters burned an effigy outside Energo-Pro's headquarters (Al Jazeera)

lenders.name: ČEZ (Czech Republic), EVN (Austria) and Energo-Pro (Czech Republic) (foreign investors)
lenders.role: The three private, foreign-controlled companies that distributed Bulgaria's electricity. EVN and other firms bought exclusive regional distribution rights in 2004 (Reuters).

cases.conditions: No loan condition is documented in the sources cited. Prosecutors found ČEZ routinely measured use at longer than monthly intervals, which Sofia Globe links to high bills; the regulator fined ČEZ and EVN for breaching licence terms.

companies.name: ČEZ Group
companies.role: Regional distributor; regulator asked to revoke its licence

companies.name: EVN Group
companies.role: Regional distributor; fined by the regulator

companies.name: Energo-Pro
companies.role: Regional distributor, Varna

cases.community: Reuters reports a jump in winter electricity bills that at times exceeded incomes, with average salaries of about 400 euros a month and pensions under half that. One retiree's bill equalled 60% of her monthly pension (Inquirer). Tens of thousands marched in cities across the country; in Varna local media put the crowd at 20,000 to 40,000 (Al Jazeera), while Reuters says about 15,000.
cases.suppression: Police and protesters clashed. Reports of injured differ: at least 15 (Inquirer), 25 taken to hospital (RNZ), several dozen (Al Jazeera). Four people were detained in Sofia (Global Voices).
cases.killed_note: No deaths caused by the companies or police are reported in the sources cited.
cases.outcome: Prime Minister Borisov promised an 8% cut in bills from March, reversing a 13% rise approved the year before (Reuters). His government resigned on 20 February 2013. He said ČEZ would lose its licence (Sofia Globe).

sources.title: Mass protests erupt across Bulgaria
Bulgarian protests for cheaper energy intensify (Reuters)
Bulgarian gov't resigns after violent protests
Bulgaria's govt resigns after national protests
Czech CEZ will lose Bulgarian distribution licence – PM
High Energy Bills Keep Bulgarians Protesting

cases.confidence_note: ČEZ says it fulfilled all its legal obligations. Bills are not measured across households in the sources cited; the figures are one retiree's bill and the 13% rise. Protests also reached wider anger over living standards. Whether the regulator finally revoked the licence was not confirmed.

lvwhy.priv: Power distribution held by three foreign-controlled companies.
lvwhy.prices: A 13% rise and winter bills that at times exceeded incomes.

cases.title: Georgian Manganese, Chiatura and Shukruti

lenders.name: Stemcor (UK), then Privat Group (Ukraine), then Georgian American Alloys (foreign investors)
lenders.role: A Stemcor subsidiary, the only bidder, won the 2006 auction of the state manganese assets. Stemcor sold 75% to Privat Group that year, and in 2013 Privat moved the company to Georgian American Alloys. As of February 2022 Igor Kolomoisky held the majority (Green Alternative profile on the Business & Human Rights Resource Centre site).

companies.name: Georgian American Alloys
companies.role: Parent of Georgian Manganese; registered in the United States, with the operating holding registered in Luxembourg (Green Alternative)

cases.community: Residents of Shukruti say mining has cracked houses and opened sinkholes; one said, "Houses are crumbling above our heads" (JAMnews). A rights monitor says the homes were damaged (OC Media); these sources give no count of damaged homes. As of November 2019 a promised commission had not led to payments.
cases.suppression: In May 2021 three residents sewed their mouths shut and ten others went on hunger strike. The mayor did not allow residents to put up a tent (JAMnews). Reporting in 2025 mentions surveillance, intimidation and detentions of protesters (Journalismfund).
cases.killed_note: Two workers named or described by OC Media: Zaza Abramishvili died in a tunnel collapse at the Shukruti mine in March 2018, and a worker fell to his death at the Chiatura processing plant in April 2017. No total for mine deaths was found in the pages cited.
cases.outcome: A court appointed a special manager on 11 May 2017 and extended this through May 2023. Fines recorded for safety and permit breaches were mostly small, for example 5,000 lari in 2012. A ₾200 million (about $82 million) Revenue Service fine was overturned on appeal in 2017, and the service was ordered to reopen the case (OC Media).

cases.title: AES Telasi Disconnections, Tbilisi

lenders.name: AES Corporation (United States) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Came to Georgia in 1998 (IWPR; the Wilson Center says the sale was in 1999) and owned 75% of Tbilisi's electricity distributor, AES Telasi. Agreed to sell it to Russia's UES in 2003 (Civil Georgia).

cases.conditions: No loan condition is documented in the sources cited.

companies.name: AES Corporation
companies.role: 75% owner of AES Telasi until 2003 (Civil Georgia)

cases.community: The rate per kWh was 6 tetri before AES took over and rose to 13.7 tetri (IWPR). The $24 monthly bill was about half the average Georgian's monthly income, and nearly 90% of customers were refusing to pay in 1999 (PBS). AES first disconnected non-paying customers en masse, including the airport and a military base (PBS; Wilson Center). Customers took to the streets, and anger turned to rioting (PBS). In winter 2001 the city had power for three or four hours a day.
cases.killed_note: No deaths caused by the company are reported in the sources cited.
cases.outcome: Georgia's Constitutional Court ruled that high electricity rates violated the constitutional rights of most citizens, and set the rate at 12.6 tetri until a new tariff was fixed (IWPR, undated). In August 2003 AES agreed to sell to UES without disclosing the price; charges tied to the sale contributed to a $129 million net loss that quarter (Civil Georgia; Power Engineering).

cases.title: Zarafshon Gold Mine, Khumgaron
cases.point: Panjakent, the district town; Khumgaron village lies near the Zarafshon mine (approximate)

lenders.name: Zijin Mining (China) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Took a 70% stake in the Zarafshon mine in 2007; the Tajik government holds 30%. The mine produces about 70% of Tajikistan's gold (RFE/RL).

companies.name: Zijin Mining
companies.role: 70% owner of JV Zarafshon

cases.community: About 150 people live in Khumgaron. One resident showed deeds for farmland where refineries were built and says it was used without her permission. A 2022 letter from residents to the President's Office described worsening health, including stillbirths; the Health Ministry gave no statistics. The company agreed to pay $13,700 a month, about $90 per resident, until 47 farmers and their families get land; a promised road and school renovation had not started in 2023.
cases.suppression: Women who filed a complaint with Panjakent officials say they were taken to a police station and warned to stop criticising the mine (RFE/RL).
cases.outcome: In 2019 the company was fined about $1,100 for lime-plant waste in the Shing River, linked to a fish die-off. In April 2023 the Prosecutor-General announced a $1.7 million fine for about $14.6 million in environmental damage; a local official said it was because part of a refinery was built without permits. An unnamed environment official told RFE/RL his agency was ordered to overlook pollution and health issues at the mine.

sources.title: Dead Fish And Dirty Air: Chinese Firms Leave Waste As They Mine Tajikistan's Gold

cases.confidence_note: Rests mainly on one RFE/RL investigation. The fines and damage figure are official, though the damage is not detailed; health effects are residents' reports without statistics. Mine officials declined RFE/RL's requests. The Business & Human Rights Resource Centre lists a Zijin response dated 16 August 2024, whose text was not available.
cases.ecosystem: Mass fish die-off in the Shing River in 2019, linked by authorities to lime-plant waste. A cyanide-containing runoff pool lies near the mine (RFE/RL).

lvwhy.project: Gold mine and refinery beside villages and rivers.

cases.title: Kumtor Glacier Dumping and the 2013 Barskoon Clashes
cases.place: Kumtor mine and Barskoon, Issyk-Kul region, Kyrgyzstan

lenders.name: Centerra Gold (Canada) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: A 2004 deal let Centerra acquire the Cameco and Kyrgyzaltyn stakes in Kumtor in exchange for Centerra shares, leaving Kyrgyzaltyn a 33% stake in the mine, later 26% (RFE/RL). Kumtor Gold Company ran the mine.

cases.conditions: No loan condition. A 2009 agreement with Centerra allowed waste to be dumped on the glaciers (RFE/RL).

companies.name: Centerra Gold
companies.role: Owner and operator of Kumtor

cases.community: Local groups pressed Centerra to build eco-friendlier infrastructure and medical facilities (RFE/RL, 2013). A court case brought by four activists covered glacier damage and accidents that killed several workers (RFE/RL, 2021).
cases.suppression: On 31 May 2013, after protesters cut power to the mine, police arrested dozens who had seized an electricity station at Barskoon, and clashes followed with about 3,000 people. Police used tear gas; at least 55 were hurt, including 13 police officers (Health Ministry, via RFE/RL). A state of emergency with a night curfew ran to 10 June.
cases.killed_note: Uncounted. RFE/RL mentions accidents that killed several workers, with no figure.
cases.outcome: On 8 May 2021 a Bishkek district court found the company had breached environmental law by placing waste rock on glaciers and fined it 261.7 billion som. Parliament passed a law on temporary state management, and Centerra called the charges meritless and began arbitration. In April 2022 the state took over Kumtor in a settlement with Centerra. On 24 May 2022 the Bishkek City Court cancelled the fine on the company's appeal, without explanation (RFE/RL).

cases.confidence_note: The fine was 261.7 billion som: $3.1 billion by Mining.com, $3.2 billion by RFE/RL in 2022. RFE/RL's 2021 article says "about $3.2 million", which its own later report contradicts. The ruling came as the government moved to take the mine, one activist was the son of the state ecology committee's chair, and the fine was cancelled in 2022. The 2009 agreement itself allowed the dumping. This episode is separate from the 1998 cyanide spill.
cases.ecosystem: Blast waste was dumped on the Davidov and Lysiy glaciers with Kyrgyz approval, eroding them over the years (RFE/RL).
